liturgical.title: The Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ

readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
And Melchiz′edek
king of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High.
And he blessed him and said,
“Blessed be Abram by God Most High,
maker of heaven and earth;
and blessed be God Most High,
who has delivered your enemies into your hand!”
And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
Read full chapter

exegesis.summary: Melchizedek, the mysterious king-priest of Salem, brings forth bread and wine and blesses Abram in the name of God Most High. This ancient encounter, set apart from the bloody sacrifices of the patriarchs, foreshadows the unique priesthood and offering of Christ. Abram's tithe acknowledges the supremacy of a priesthood that does not arise from Levi but stands above it, pointing forward to the eternal High Priest.

patristicQuotes.quote: He taught us to offer not bread only, but wine also, to show that they who hungered and thirsted after righteousness were to be refreshed by these mysteries.

cccReferences.title: Bread and wine: Melchizedek's offering prefigures the Eucharist
Melchizedek prefigures the priesthood of Christ
God calls Abram to gather the nations

exegesis.thematicConnection: On Corpus Christi the Church reads this scene as the first dim sketch of the altar: bread and wine offered by a priest whose order Christ will fulfill, the same elements He will take, bless, and give in the Upper Room and in every Mass.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
Assurance of Victory for God’s Priest-King
A Psalm of David.
The
says to my lord:
“Sit at my right hand,
till I make your enemies your footstool.”
Read full chapter
Psalm 110:1 in all English translations

exegesis.summary: Psalm 110 is the great messianic oracle: the Lord enthrones His Anointed at His right hand and declares Him 'a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.' David, inspired by the Holy Spirit, sings of One greater than himself — the Priest-King whose reign is eternal. The Church hears in this psalm the voice of the Father addressing the risen Christ, our heavenly High Priest.

patristicQuotes.quote: David called Him Lord in the Holy Spirit; and that He is Lord, he shows by what is added: 'Till I make thine enemies thy footstool.'
God puts Christ's enemies as a footstool beneath His feet, for their salvation as well as their destruction.

cccReferences.title: David, prophet of the Messiah's prayer
The Psalter as the Word of God become prayer

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm names what Genesis only hinted at: Christ is the priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. It is His eternal priesthood, sung by David, that is made present on every altar where bread and wine become His Body and Blood.

readings.title: Second reading
readings.text:
The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread,
and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body which is for
you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
In the same way also the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
Read full chapter

exegesis.summary: Paul transmits the oldest written account of the institution of the Eucharist, received from the Lord Himself: 'This is my body... This cup is the new covenant in my blood.' These are not symbolic words but the founding decree of the New Covenant, sealed in Christ's own Blood. Every celebration of the Eucharist proclaims His death until He comes, making present the one sacrifice of Calvary.

patristicQuotes.quote: Having finished the rites of the old Passover, He passes on to the new, substituting for the flesh and blood of the lamb the Sacrament of His own Flesh and Blood in the figure of the bread and wine, being made a Priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
To eat the heavenly bread spiritually is to bring to the altar an innocent mind... it is bread, not poison. None then that eateth of this bread shall die.

cccReferences.title: The Eucharist instituted at the Last Supper
Transubstantiation: Christ truly, really, substantially present
Jesus' free offering of Himself at the Supper

exegesis.thematicConnection: Where Melchizedek offered bread and wine in figure, and David sang of the eternal Priest, Paul shows us the reality: Christ Himself, on the night He was betrayed, transformed bread and wine into His own Body and Blood. The promise is now sacrament.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text:
When the crowds learned it, they followed him; and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and cured those who had need of healing.
Now the day began to wear away; and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away, to go into the villages and country round about, to lodge and get provisions; for we are here in a lonely place.”
But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.”
For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Make them sit down in companies, about fifty each.”
And they did so, and made them all sit down.
And taking the five loaves and the two fish he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
And all ate and were satisfied. And they took up what was left over, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
Read full chapter

exegesis.summary: In a deserted place at day's end, Jesus takes five loaves and two fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them through the hands of the Twelve, and the multitude is satisfied with twelve baskets left over. The fourfold action — take, bless, break, give — is the Eucharistic gesture itself. The Lord who feeds the five thousand is the same Lord who, by the hands of His priests, feeds His Church.

patristicQuotes.quote: He distributes to them by the hands of His disciples, so honoring them that they might not forget it when the miracle was past... He himself is both the Giver of food, and the same who said, 'Let the earth bring forth.'
By the twelve baskets, as if of each of the tribes, the foundation of the faith is spread abroad.

cccReferences.title: The multiplication of loaves prefigures the Eucharist
The Twelve share in Christ's mission

exegesis.thematicConnection: The miracle gathers up all that has come before: bread blessed and given by the true Priest-King, the superabundance of the new covenant, food multiplied through apostolic hands. The twelve baskets are the Church's perpetual abundance — the Eucharist, never depleted, given to every generation.

synthesis.title: The Priest Forever Gives Us His Body and Blood
synthesis.body: On this Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, the Church gathers four moments of revelation into one luminous mystery. Melchizedek emerges from the dawn of salvation history bearing bread and wine, blessing Abram in the name of God Most High — a priesthood older than Levi, pointing beyond itself. David's psalm names what Genesis only shadowed: there is a Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, enthroned at the Father's right hand. In Paul's letter that eternal Priest steps into time on the night He was betrayed, takes bread and the cup, and speaks the words that change the world: 'This is my body... This is the new covenant in my blood.' And in Luke's deserted place, the Lord takes, blesses, breaks, and gives through the hands of the Twelve, feeding the multitude with abundance to spare. The Church proclaims today that these are not four stories but one: the bread and wine of Melchizedek, the priesthood of the Psalms, the words of institution, and the miracle of the loaves are all fulfilled at this altar. Christ, truly, really, and substantially present under the consecrated species, is the food that does not perish. We who eat this bread proclaim His death until He comes — and we are made one Body in Him.
